text: Priority is not a field an agent should just type into by feel. It's calculated — and implementing Incident Management well means knowing exactly how that calculation works, when to trust it, and when to let an agent override it deliberately instead of by habit.

Impact and Urgency are the two ITIL inputs: Impact is how many people or services are affected, Urgency is how fast the business needs it fixed. Platform Fundamentals' Choice Lists lesson showed you how a choice field gets its value, backed by a sys_choice entry — Impact and Urgency are exactly that kind of field, each with its own set of labeled values.

ServiceNow ships a real table for turning those two choices into Priority automatically: priority_lookup_rule. Each row maps one Impact-and-Urgency combination to a Priority value — Impact 1 and Urgency 1 to Critical, Impact 3 and Urgency 3 to Low, and every combination in between across the full grid. Set Impact and Urgency on a record, and Priority fills in on its own, with no separate click and no incident left with Priority blank.

That's a genuine implementation choice, not a default to accept blindly. A calculated Priority keeps prioritization consistent across every agent and every shift, which is exactly what any SLA definition later in this path depends on. Allowing manual override gives room to escalate a case the matrix under-weights, but every override is one more thing an auditor will ask you to justify. Most mature implementations keep the lookup rule as the default and log every override rather than disable the calculation entirely.

Calculated for consistency, override logged for flexibility, and the matrix itself reviewed against the business's own real definitions of Impact and Urgency before it ever goes live.
